input.question: How allergy shots work.
input.ground_truth: They inject you with a *really tiny* amount of the allergen at first, then subsequent shots up the dosage a little bit at a time. It exposes your body to the allergen in such a way that it never freaks out and eventually realizes that there isn't actually a threat.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How allergy shots work.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a tiny bug that doesn’t like you and makes you sneeze and get itchy when it comes near you. That’s like having an allergy.

Allergy shots are like giving your body a tiny, tiny bit of that bug (but it’s not really the bug, just a part of it that helps your body learn). You get these shots little by little, over time.

Every time you get a shot, your body learns, “Hey, this is not so scary!” and gets stronger, so next time the real bug comes, your body knows how to fight it better and doesn’t get as upset.

So, allergy shots help your body learn to not get so mad when it sees the thing that makes you sneeze or itch.
